AmiBSDNet is a TCP/IP network stack for AmigaOS 3.1 and later, built
from the networking code of the NetBSD 11 kernel: the real BSD TCP/IP,
IPv4 and IPv6 implementation, running as a "rump kernel" on top of
Exec. Programs use it through the standard bsdsocket.library (AmiTCP /
Roadshow API), so existing Amiga network software works without
changes.

Requirements
------------
- AmigaOS 3.1 or later (the installer stops on an older system)
- a 68020 or better CPU; a PiStorm (Emu68) is the main target
- Fast RAM: the stack uses about 3.5 MB, all of it Fast RAM (no Chip RAM)
- a network card with a SANA-II driver. On a PiStorm, according to the
  drivers' own documentation and sources:
  - wifipi.device (Wi-Fi): a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, 3B, 3A+, 3B+, 4B or
    CM4, and the Wi-Fi firmware for it in DEVS:Firmware (from
    Emu68-tools)
  - genet.device (Ethernet): only a Raspberry Pi 4B or CM4 (PiStorm32-
    lite), Emu68 1.1 alpha.1 or newer, LIBS:gic400.library, and
    genet.device 2.2 or newer
  Before it touches one of these drivers AmiBSDNet checks the Pi model
  (and for genet.device its Ethernet) in Emu68's device tree, the
  firmware files, gic400.library (in memory, in Emu68's ROM or in LIBS:)
  and the version in genet.device's file; the Emu68 version itself is
  not checked. It leaves a driver alone whose requirements are not met
  (the installer and the log say why; see Logs). WinUAE: uaenet.device; Zorro
  cards such as the A2065, Ariadne or X-Surf: their own driver
- no other TCP/IP stack running at the same time (the installer offers
  to take an installed one out of the boot)

What has been tested
--------------------
This version has been tested in the WinUAE emulator only: installed
with the Workbench 3.2 Installer (Kickstart 3.2.2, 68040), with WinUAE's
uaenet.device. It has not been tested on PiStorm hardware: not with
wifipi.device, genet.device or PaulaNET, and not with Zorro network
cards. What this text says about those drivers comes from their
documentation and sources.

Installation
------------
Double-click "Install". The installer asks, in this order:

1. If AmiBSDNet is installed already: "Install again (update)" or
   "Uninstall AmiBSDNet" (see Uninstalling).

2. If another TCP/IP stack is installed (Roadshow, Miami, AmiTCP,
   Genesis, or any bsdsocket.library on disk):

     Switch       (the default) its startup lines in S:Startup-Sequence
                  and S:User-Startup are commented out ("; [AmiBSDNet]
                  ..."), and its WBStartup items and
                  LIBS:bsdsocket.library are moved to
                  SYS:Storage/AmiBSDNet-Disabled. This is a trial (see
                  below).
     Keep it      nothing is changed.

   If it is Roadshow and you chose Switch, a second question asks
   whether to remove Roadshow completely instead. Its default is No:
   removing is done only if you choose it. Roadshow's programs are
   then deleted and its settings moved to SYS:Storage/AmiBSDNet-Roadshow
   (see "NetCtrl REMOVEROADSHOW"); there is no trial and no way back
   except reinstalling Roadshow. At the Novice user level this question
   is not asked (a Novice installation asks nothing), so Roadshow is
   only switched; the installer's icon starts it at the Average level.

3. If there is a C:Ping that is not AmiBSDNet's: whether to replace it
   with AmiBSDNet's Ping (default: keep yours).

4. Where to create the AmiBSDNet drawer (default SYS:): the drawer
   "AmiBSDNet" is created there, with this documentation and the
   status icon.

5. If a PaulaNET adapter is plugged in: whether to copy its driver to
   DEVS:Networks (see PaulaNET).

6. If AmiBSDNet's network settings exist already (an earlier
   installation): keep them as they are (the default; questions 7 to
   10 are then skipped), or enter them again.

7. The network adapters. The installer finds them by itself (every
   SANA-II driver in DEVS:Networks, and drivers built into ROM such as
   WinUAE's uaenet.device) and tells Ethernet from Wi-Fi. If you have
   both, both are set up. If none is found, or you want another one,
   you choose the driver file, its unit number and whether it is Wi-Fi.
   If only PaulaNET was found, you can use only PaulaNET.

8. For Wi-Fi: whether to replace existing Wi-Fi settings
   (ENVARC:Sys/Wireless.prefs), the network name (SSID), whether it is
   a hidden network, and the passphrase. Leave the name empty to choose
   the network later from the status icon.

9. Whether the network uses DHCP (most do) or a fixed address.

10. The host name of this Amiga (letters, digits and '-'); then, for a
    fixed address, the address with its prefix length (for example
    192.168.1.20/24), the router (gateway) and the DNS server. The
    installer checks that they are valid IPv4 addresses.

11. In Average and Expert mode: a confirmation of the lines added to
    S:User-Startup:

        Run >NIL: C:SerialShell AUTO
        C:AmiBSDNet

    (The first starts the Shell on the serial port if it is switched
    on; it comes first so that it is there even if the network does
    not start.)

12. The Shell on the serial port (see SerialShell): whether to switch
    it on (default: no). If it is on already, whether to keep it on
    (default: yes).

13. Whether to show the status icon on the Workbench at every boot
    (copies AmiBSDNetStatus to SYS:WBStartup; default: yes).

Switching from the other stack happens last, after everything else is
installed. The stack starts in the background; boot is not delayed
while it waits for a DHCP server.

The PiStorm's Wi-Fi driver (wifipi.device and DEVS:Firmware) is never
touched: it belongs to your Emu68 installation (it relies on Emu68's
devicetree.resource). AmiBSDNet uses the one that is installed; if
there is none, install it from Emu68-tools, preferably of the same
release as your Emu68.

The switch is a trial. After the next boot AmiBSDNet has three minutes
to get connected. If it does, the switch stays. If it does not, it goes
back by itself ("NetCtrl FALLBACK"): the other stack is put back,
AmiBSDNet is taken out of the boot, its logs are saved in
SYS:Storage/AmiBSDNet-Logs, and a requester asks you to reboot. You are
never left without a network: a trial boot that ends without a
connection (the machine hangs, crashes or is reset before AmiBSDNet has
connected) also counts as failed, and the next boot goes back by
itself. So after switching, leave the machine running until the status
icon shows an address. "NetCtrl FALLBACK" also goes back by hand at any
time; once you are happy with AmiBSDNet (after the trial), "NetCtrl
REMOVEOTHERS" deletes the other stack's startup lines for good (also
the disabled ones); its parked files stay in
SYS:Storage/AmiBSDNet-Disabled until you delete that drawer.

The startup files are saved as S:<name>.amibsdnet-bak before the first
change. Afterwards the installer checks again and tells you if anything
of the other stack would still be started at boot. AmiBSDNet itself
does not start while another stack is running (and never stops the
rest of S:User-Startup).

The install log
---------------
S:AmiBSDNet-Install.log lists the files and drawers the installer
created, one "FILE <path>" line each; a file also has its size and
CRC32 as the installer left it ("FILE <path> <size> <crc32>"), and the
uninstaller deletes such a file only if it is still unchanged. Files
that were there before (your own) are not listed. Listed are: the
programs in C: (C:Ping only if it was not there or you chose to replace
it), C:WirelessManager if it was not there, the AmiBSDNet drawer (no
size and CRC32 for a drawer and the drawer's icon) and its files, the
status icon copied to SYS:WBStartup, DEVS:Internet/hosts (and
DEVS:Internet) if there was none, and ENVARC:Sys/Wireless.prefs and
ENV:Sys/Wireless.prefs if there were none.

Not in the log: the lines in S:User-Startup (the log names the block,
";BEGIN AmiBSDNet"), the settings in ENVARC:AmiBSDNet and ENV:AmiBSDNet
(AmiBSDNet.conf, SerialShell, Trial, and Installed, where the installer
notes which files are AmiBSDNet's), the PaulaNET.device copied to
DEVS:Networks, and the changes made when switching from another stack
(see above).

While the Amiga starts
----------------------
For the first minute after a boot, AmiBSDNet, SerialShell and the
status icon each show what they are doing in a small window at the
bottom of the screen; the windows close by themselves. If the Amiga
freezes while they start, that window shows the step that froze it
(take a picture of it).

A start that never finished (the Amiga froze, or was switched off in
that first minute) is not tried again at the next boot: that one boot
comes up without it, and a requester on the Workbench says so. The boot
after that starts it normally again.

Uninstalling
------------
Run the installer again and choose "Uninstall AmiBSDNet" (or type
"NetCtrl UNINSTALL" in a Shell). It takes AmiBSDNet out of
S:User-Startup first; if that file cannot be changed, nothing is
removed. It then deletes what the install log lists (a file with a
size and CRC32 only if it is unchanged: a hosts file or Wireless.prefs
you edited stays), the programs C:AmiBSDNet, C:NetCtrl and
C:SerialShell, the status icon in
SYS:WBStartup, the settings (ENVARC:AmiBSDNet and ENV:AmiBSDNet),
SYS:Storage/AmiBSDNet-Logs, and finally the log itself. If you saved
your own files in a drawer the installer created, the drawer and those
files stay. A TCP/IP stack that AmiBSDNet was switched from is put
back. Your drivers are not touched; a PaulaNET.device the installer
copied to DEVS:Networks stays. NetCtrl's report (whether everything
was removed, and what was kept) is in T:AmiBSDNet-Uninstall.txt. Reboot afterwards: the stack that is still
in memory goes then.

Ethernet and Wi-Fi together
---------------------------
Ethernet and Wi-Fi are separate interfaces that work at the same time,
each with its own address from its own network. Internet traffic goes
out through Ethernet while its cable is connected and through Wi-Fi
otherwise; the switch happens by itself when the cable is plugged in or
pulled. The name servers of both are used.

Cable and Wi-Fi changes
-----------------------
Nothing has to be started by hand. With DHCP, AmiBSDNet keeps asking
for an address in the background until it gets one, so a cable plugged
in or a router switched on after boot is picked up by itself. Drivers
that report link changes (SANA-II link events, e.g. Wi-Fi association)
make it react at once: the address is released when the link goes and
fetched again when it returns. The status icon shows "No cable" or
"No Wi-Fi" while there is no link.

Wi-Fi
-----
Wireless drivers such as Emu68's wifipi.device associate with the
network; the WPA handshake is done by WirelessManager (Neil Cafferkey's
wpa_supplicant port, installed to C:WirelessManager), which reads
ENV:Sys/Wireless.prefs. WirelessManager is included in this package
(see ThirdParty.txt for its authors and licence); the Wi-Fi driver is
the one installed with Emu68. AmiBSDNet starts WirelessManager itself
for a Wi-Fi interface if it is not already running. The installer asks
for the network name and passphrase; to change networks later,
double-click the status icon and choose Wi-Fi...: the window lists the
networks in range (strongest first), and Connect stores the network,
restarts WirelessManager and fetches a new address. A scan can be
stopped with Close; it gives up by itself after 60 seconds of
scanning. The time the driver takes to get ready first counts a fifth
of that, so in all it gives up after at most 5 minutes.

The installer cannot set up a network whose name contains a '"', or a
passphrase that contains one.

Hidden networks (ones that do not show their name): answer Yes to the
installer's question, which adds "scan_ssid=1" to the network's entry
in Wireless.prefs (as WirelessManager's manual describes). Connect in
the Wi-Fi window and the Settings window write the entry of the network
anew with its name and passphrase; its other lines (such as
"scan_ssid=1") are kept. For a network whose security the driver does
not report, Connect with an empty passphrase keeps the saved one.

WirelessManager's manual (in the prism2v2 archive on Aminet) says that
a textual WPA/WPA2 passphrase causes a start-up delay of up to several
minutes on a slow CPU; a hexadecimal key, computed with the
wpa_passphrase command from that archive, avoids it (it has to be
computed again if the network name changes).

The status icon shows "Net: No Wi-Fi" until WirelessManager has joined
the network; DHCP starts as soon as it has. WirelessManager's messages
are in SYS:Storage/AmiBSDNet-Logs/WirelessManager.log. For more of
them, type

    SetEnv SAVE AmiBSDNet/Debug 1

and reboot (SAVE keeps the variable in ENVARC: across the reboot;
"UnSetEnv SAVE AmiBSDNet/Debug" switches it off again). If the status
window says "DRIVER NOT USED", the driver named in the settings is not
in DEVS:Networks, or it could not set up its hardware (the log says
which; see Logs). A driver that cannot set up its hardware - genet.device on
a Pi without working Ethernet, for one - gets no further commands.

PaulaNET
--------
PaulaNET (https://github.com/RobSmithDev/PaulaNET) is Wi-Fi through the
floppy port, using a Raspberry Pi Pico W or Pico 2 W. AmiBSDNet uses it
by itself whenever it is plugged in: at every start it looks for
PaulaNET.device in DEVS:, DEVS:Networks or on the adapter's own
PaulaNET: disk, and adds it as one more DHCP interface, used for the
Internet only when no other interface is connected. Without the adapter
it stays hidden. The Wi-Fi network is set up with the PaulaNET Config
program on the PaulaNET disk, not in AmiBSDNet.

PaulaNET.device is not included in this package (its author has not
published it under a licence that allows that). The installer copies it
from the PaulaNET disk to DEVS:Networks, reads it twice and compares,
and copies it again if the copy differs. It recognises the official
versions 1.0 and 1.1.

The PaulaNET row of the Settings window: "Verify" (off by default)
makes the stack use only an official version of the driver, or one
whose CRC is in the "CRC" field (up to four, separated by spaces).
Check shows which version is installed; for one AmiBSDNet does not know
(a newer release, or a damaged copy) it shows the CRC and, with Verify
on, adds it to the field: Save accepts it. A driver that fails the check
shows as "DRIVER FAILED THE CHECK" / "Net: Bad driver". "PaulaNET" off
stops AmiBSDNet from adding the adapter. PaulaNET always uses DHCP.

The status icon
---------------
AmiBSDNetStatus puts an icon on the Workbench showing whether you are
online and your address (or "No cable", "No Wi-Fi", "Connecting").
Double-click it for a status window with Go Online / Go Offline,
Reconnect, Wi-Fi... (for Wi-Fi interfaces) and Settings.... The same
windows are in the Workbench Tools menu: "AmiBSDNet..." and "AmiBSDNet
Settings...".

The Settings window holds the whole configuration: the Ethernet and
Wi-Fi drivers (Detect finds them), automatic (DHCP) or fixed address,
gateway, DNS server, host name, and the Wi-Fi network and passphrase
(Scan... lists the networks in range), PaulaNET, and the Shell on the
serial port with its speed (see SerialShell). Save stores the settings
and applies them at once, without a reboot; Use applies them until the
next reboot. A fixed address stays on the interface that has it in the
configuration; if none has one, it is used for Ethernet if there is an
Ethernet adapter, else for Wi-Fi. With Automatic (DHCP) the window
takes its gateway line and its name server (the first "nameserver"
line) out of the configuration; further "nameserver" lines stay, and
are used after the DHCP server's.

It is also the "AmiBSDNet" commodity in Exchange: Show opens the status
window, Enable / Disable switch the network online / offline. Tool
types: STACKCMD=<command to start the stack> (default C:AmiBSDNet),
INTERVAL=<seconds between updates>.

Logs
----
AmiBSDNet writes its log to SYS:Storage/AmiBSDNet-Logs/AmiBSDNet.log,
and WirelessManager's messages go to
SYS:Storage/AmiBSDNet-Logs/WirelessManager.log. Both are on the disk,
so they are still there after a reboot or a power-off; each start
begins them anew. They can be read while the stack runs:

    Type SYS:Storage/AmiBSDNet-Logs/AmiBSDNet.log

If that drawer cannot be written, the logs go to T:AmiBSDNet.log and
T:WirelessManager.log instead, which are lost at a reboot.

Commands
--------
AmiBSDNet [CONFIG=<file>] [LOG=<file>] [DEBUG]
    Starts the stack. Configuration defaults to
    ENV:AmiBSDNet/AmiBSDNet.conf, the log to
    SYS:Storage/AmiBSDNet-Logs/AmiBSDNet.log (see Logs).

NetCtrl [STATUS|ONLINE|OFFLINE|RECONFIG|WAIT|PROBE|CHECK|...]
        [TIMEOUT=<s>]
    STATUS    interfaces, addresses, traffic counters, name servers
    ONLINE    bring the network up
    OFFLINE   take the network down
    RECONFIG  re-read the configuration file
    WAIT      wait until the network is up (for scripts)

NetCtrl PROBE
    Lists the network adapters and whether each is Ethernet or Wi-Fi;
    sets the variables AmiBSDNet/Ethernet and AmiBSDNet/WiFi (and
    AmiBSDNet/PaulaNET to the PaulaNET driver's file, if there is one).

NetCtrl CHECKDRIVER [FILE=<driver>]
    Checks a PaulaNET.device (default: the one that would be loaded):
    official version, accepted CRC, unknown, or damaged. Sets
    AmiBSDNet/DriverCheck, AmiBSDNet/DriverCRC, AmiBSDNet/DriverVersion.

NetCtrl CHECK
    Lists other installed TCP/IP stacks and what of them is still
    started at boot.

NetCtrl DISABLEOTHERS | REMOVEOTHERS | RESTOREOTHERS | FALLBACK
    Takes other TCP/IP stacks out of the boot (can be undone), removes
    their startup entries and files, or undoes DISABLEOTHERS. FALLBACK
    goes back completely: the other stack comes back, AmiBSDNet is
    taken out of the boot, and its logs are saved in
    SYS:Storage/AmiBSDNet-Logs. Reboot afterwards. DISABLEOTHERS and
    REMOVEOTHERS change nothing unless AmiBSDNet is started from
    S:User-Startup, and REMOVEOTHERS also nothing while the switch is
    still a trial (until AmiBSDNet has connected once).

NetCtrl REENABLE
    The way back from FALLBACK: the lines of AmiBSDNet's block in
    S:User-Startup that FALLBACK commented out are active again (the
    other stack is not taken out of the boot again: use DISABLEOTHERS
    for that). Reboot afterwards.

NetCtrl PANIC | PANICTHREAD
    For testing only: makes the kernel stop with a panic, on the
    stack's own task or on a kernel thread, so that what follows can be
    tried out. The stack refuses it (NetCtrl says "failed") unless it
    was started with DEBUG. After it the network is gone until the next
    reboot.

NetCtrl KEEPCONF FILE=<out> [NOAUTODETECT]
    For the installer: writes the PaulaNET lines ("paulanet ...",
    "autodetect ...") of ENVARC:AmiBSDNet/AmiBSDNet.conf to <out>
    (empty if there are none). NOAUTODETECT leaves out "autodetect".

NetCtrl CHECKSUM FILE=<file>
    For the installer: prints "<size> <crc32>" of a file (size in
    decimal, CRC-32 as 8 lowercase hex digits) and sets
    AmiBSDNet/FileSum to it.

NetCtrl FINDROADSHOW | REMOVEROADSHOW
    FINDROADSHOW lists the files of the Roadshow archive that are where
    its installation puts them on SYS:, and the comments that mention
    Roadshow in S:Startup-Sequence and S:User-Startup. REMOVEROADSHOW
    removes Roadshow's startup lines and WBStartup items, deletes its
    own commands, PPP drivers and catalogs, moves its settings and
    scripts (S:Network-Startup, the firewall and PPP scripts,
    DEVS:NetInterfaces, DEVS:Internet but hosts and services,
    ENVARC:Roadshow) to
    SYS:Storage/AmiBSDNet-Roadshow - and LIBS:bsdsocket.library and
    LIBS:usergroup.library too if no other TCP/IP stack is installed -
    removes those comments (copies: S:*.amibsdnet-rs), and then looks
    again. There is no trial and no way back except reinstalling
    Roadshow. Commands with general names (ping, ftp...) and anything
    in other places are left alone. REMOVEROADSHOW changes nothing
    unless AmiBSDNet is started from S:User-Startup. The installer's
    "Remove Roadshow" question does this.

NetCtrl UNINSTALL
    Removes AmiBSDNet (see Uninstalling).

SerialShell [START|STOP|STATUS|AUTO] [BAUD=<n>] [UNIT=<n>]
            [DEVICE=<name>]
    A Shell on the serial port, for a terminal program on another
    computer (null-modem cable): 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit, no
    XON/XOFF and no RTS/CTS, 19200 baud unless BAUD= says otherwise
    (serial.device unit 0). The system's Serial preferences are not
    changed. START runs it ("Run >NIL: C:SerialShell START"); after
    EndShell a new Shell starts. STOP ends it. AUTO, in S:User-Startup,
    starts it if it is switched on: "Shell on the serial port" and its
    speed in the Settings window (ENV:AmiBSDNet/SerialShell holds the
    baud rate). On the terminal: Backspace, Ctrl-X (line), Ctrl-C
    (break), Ctrl-\ (end of file). Set the terminal to the same speed,
    8N1, no flow control.

Ping HOST [COUNT=<n>]
    Send ICMP echo requests.

Configuration file
------------------
ENVARC:AmiBSDNet/AmiBSDNet.conf (copied to ENV: at boot), one item per
line, '#' starts a comment:

    hostname   amiga
    interface  sana0 genet.device 0 dhcp
    interface  sana1 wifipi.device 0 dhcp wifi
    # or a fixed address:
    # interface  sana0 genet.device 0 address 192.168.1.20/24
    # gateway    192.168.1.1
    # nameserver 192.168.1.1
    domain     home.lan
    # PaulaNET (see above); all optional:
    # autodetect off             do not add the PaulaNET adapter
    # paulanet   verify on       use only a known PaulaNET.device
    # paulanet   crc 1a2b3c4d    also accept this one (up to four)

Up to four interfaces (sana0 ... sana3) can be configured; the first
one that is connected carries the Internet traffic. "wifi" marks a
Wi-Fi interface for the Settings window (the stack also detects it from
the driver). With DHCP, the router and name servers come from the DHCP
server.

Host names are looked up in DEVS:Internet/hosts first, then with DNS.

Limitations of this version
---------------------------
- The stack cannot be unloaded once started (NetCtrl OFFLINE takes the
  network down); a reboot removes it.
- IPv6 is built in, but it is not configured automatically.
- The packet filter has no channels: the bpf_* calls fail with ENXIO.
  ChangeRouteTagList and the IP filter calls (ipf_*) fail with ENOSYS.
  AddInterfaceTagList takes only IFA_LimitMTU, and IFA_IPType and
  IFA_ARPType with their defaults (2048, 2054); other tags fail with
  EINVAL.
- gethostname returns the configured host name ("hostname" in
  AmiBSDNet.conf, "amiga" when there is none); it does not look the
  interface address up in the hosts file or DNS, or read the HOSTNAME
  variable, as the Roadshow autodoc describes (bsdsocket.doc,
  gethostname, NOTES).
- genet.device does not report a cable being pulled or plugged in, so
  AmiBSDNet cannot see it either; and genet waits 6 seconds for a link
  when it is set up: without a cable plugged in at boot it is not used
  until the next boot.
- PaulaNET.device, when installed, looks for its adapter on the floppy
  ports at every start (that is how the driver works).
